item_name: Where LFR van locations are published, live or otherwise
operator: Three police forces publish (or fail to publish) London LFR deployment locations, and they do it in three different ways. Metropolitan Police - the largest operator, roughly two van deployments a week plus the Croydon static cameras, publishing a detailed retrospective record and nothing forward-looking on its own website. British Transport Police - the smallest London operator but the most transparent, publishing both an 'Upcoming deployments' notice and a deployment register on one page. City of London Police - operates no LFR of its own and therefore publishes nothing. Alongside them sit the unofficial channels that actually carry same-day notice: the Met's borough Basic Command Unit accounts on X, local press, and campaign groups (Big Brother Watch, Liberty, StopWatch) who amplify and criticise but run no tracker of their own.
vendor: Not a vendor question, but relevant to why the records are comparable: the Met, BTP and South Wales Police all run NEC NeoFace, and the Met and BTP both publish a minimum match threshold of 0.64 in their deployment records, so the two London registers can be read side by side. No third-party publisher, aggregator or vendor of LFR deployment data exists for London; there is no commercial or open-data product in this space.
london_coverage_summary: Every channel that carries a London LFR deployment location was checked: the Met's own facial recognition page and its four deployment-record PDFs, BTP's LFR page and register, City of London Police's site, the Greater London Authority and Mayor's Question archive, the London Datastore, Big Brother Watch, Liberty, Privacy International, OpenStreetMap-derived camera maps, GitHub, local and national press, and the Met's borough policing accounts on X. The result is a clean split. Where a van HAS BEEN is published in real detail - street-level location, date, duration to the minute, watchlist size, alert counts, arrests and estimated faces seen - but weeks to months after the fact. Where a van WILL BE is announced, if at all, by a text post on a borough policing X account on or about the day, and by BTP on its own website for the transport network. Where a van IS RIGHT NOW is published nowhere, by anyone, in any form. No live map of LFR van positions exists, official or third-party, and no one is building one.
camera_count_claimed: Not applicable - this item is about publication channels, not installations, so no operator claims a camera count here. The relevant volumetric figures are about deployments and about the records themselves: the Met's published record contains 231 deployment rows for 2025 alone across roughly 110 distinct location labels, and about 447 deployments across all 32 boroughs since 2020 per the London Assembly's analysis of the same records; BTP's register held 19 deployments across 8 London station sites between 11 February and 11 August 2026. For hardware, the Met's 2025 annual report states deployments are 'typically carried out twice a week using two dedicated vans', and the January 2026 policing White Paper promised 40 further LFR vans nationally.
fixed_vs_mobile: The publication regime differs sharply between the two, and this matters for anyone mapping it. Van deployments are transient - a van parks for four to six hours and leaves - so the only durable public artefact is the retrospective record; there is no location to map on any given day and no status to poll. Fixed installations are the opposite: the Met's Croydon static cameras on North End and London Road were announced publicly before installation, are physically permanent on street furniture, and appear in the deployment record as 'North End, Croydon' rows from 1 October 2025 onward. The West End and Soho static rollout announced by Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley on 24 June 2026 for delivery by the end of 2026 will produce more of these, with further locations to be chosen with councils from 2027 - meaning that over time a growing share of London LFR becomes mappable as fixed points, while the van half remains unmappable in advance by design. BTP's transport deployments are a third category: temporary camera masts on station concourses, neither fixed nor vehicle-mounted, published station by station.
geographic_concentration: From the Met's own deployment records, as analysed in Zoe Garbett AM's February 2026 London Assembly report: since 2020 the Met has deployed LFR in every one of the 32 London boroughs, but Westminster (75 deployments), Croydon (55) and Newham (35) dominate, followed by Camden (20), Southwark (23), Haringey (20), Greenwich (20), Hammersmith and Fulham (16), Barking and Dagenham (15), Lewisham (15) and Wandsworth (15). At the other end, Barnet has had 1, Bexley 2, Merton 2 and Richmond 2. Those three leading boroughs also lead on deployments per 100,000 residents - Westminster 36.72, Croydon 14.08, Newham 9.97 - so the concentration is not simply a footfall effect. The same report found 263 deployments in wards with a lower-than-London-average White population against 180 in higher-than-average wards, and 145 against 86 in 2025 alone. Recurring street-level sites named repeatedly in the 2025 record include Powis Street Woolwich, High Street North East Ham, Stratford Broadway, Oxford Circus, Rye Lane Peckham, Wembley Central, Kilburn High Road, High Street Ilford and North End Croydon.
last_confirmed_active_date: 3 September 2026 - the most recent London LFR deployment this research could date from a publication channel, announced on the Westminster Police / Central West BCU account (@MPSWestminster) as a deployment to crime hotspots in Westminster borough on Thursday 3 September 2026, and picked up by Big Brother Watch on X the same day. That is three days before the 6 September 2026 date of this research, and it is a good illustration of the whole problem: the announcement exists, it is dated, it names a borough - and it is a social media post that will be invisible in a week, carries no street, no coordinate and no time window, and is not collected anywhere. [uncertain - the 3 September 2026 Westminster deployment is attested by search-result metadata for the @MPSWestminster post and a same-day Big Brother Watch repost, but the post itself could not be retrieved directly (x.com returns HTTP 402 to automated fetches), and it will not appear in a Met deployment record until the 2026 record is next updated]
evidence_of_current_activity: The publication regime is demonstrably live on all three of its channels. Official retrospective: the Met's facial recognition page carries a 'Live Facial Recognition - Deployment Record 2026' PDF alongside the 2025, 2023-24 and 2020-22 records, so the archive is being maintained into the current year. Official prospective: BTP's LFR page carried a live 'Upcoming deployments' entry reading 'Tuesday 11 August - London Victoria Underground station' when captured on 11 August 2026, and its deployment register was updated to include that deployment by 15 August 2026. Unofficial prospective: borough policing accounts on X posted deployment notices for Croydon (15 January 2025), Haringey (5 November) and Westminster (3 September 2026), the Haringey post in the future tense - 'On 5th November, we are deploying Live Facial Recognition Technology to crime hotspots in #Haringey borough'. The Met's own Live Facial Recognition Annual Report 2025, published 31 October 2025, describes the practice in its own words: when deploying to a new location officers 'engage with local communities and businesses, display signage on the day, and announce the deployment via social media'.
known_pauses_or_withdrawals: One channel has quietly disappeared and one has gone stale, and both matter for anyone relying on these sources. (1) The Met's old advice-section LFR page at https://www.met.police.uk/advice/advice-and-information/facial-recognition/live-facial-recognition/ now returns 404 or redirects; archived captures from 2026 show 302 then 404. Everything moved to https://www.met.police.uk/police-forces/metropolitan-police/areas/about-us/about-the-met/facial-recognition-technology/ , and no upcoming-deployment listing survived the move. (2) The legacy deployment-record URL https://www.met.police.uk/SysSiteAssets/media/downloads/force-content/met/advice/lfr/deployment-records/lfr-deployment-grid.pdf was still resolving on 31 July 2026 but served a truncated 2025 file whose last row is 11/07/2025 - a stale copy nearly thirteen months out of date sitting at a URL that older articles and FOI responses still link to. Anyone building a scraper against the Met's deployment records must target the current per-year filenames, not the old grid. Nothing has been withdrawn on the BTP side; its register is young, complete and updated during the trial. Big Brother Watch's own in-page deployment table at https://bigbrotherwatch.org.uk/blog/understanding-live-facial-recognition-statistics/ has not been extended past 2023 and should not be treated as current.
publication_channel: Nine channels, in descending order of usefulness. (1) METROPOLITAN POLICE DEPLOYMENT RECORDS - the single most valuable source in this survey. https://www.met.police.uk/police-forces/metropolitan-police/areas/about-us/about-the-met/facial-recognition-technology/ , under the heading 'Deployment records', links four PDFs: Deployment Record 2026 ( https://www.met.police.uk/SysSiteAssets/media/downloads/force-content/met/advice/lfr/deployment-records/live-facial-recognition-deployment-record-2026 ), 2025 ( https://www.met.police.uk/SysSiteAssets/media/downloads/force-content/met/advice/lfr/deployment-records/live-facial-recognition-deployment-record-2025.pdf ), 2023 to 2024 ( https://www.met.police.uk/SysSiteAssets/media/downloads/force-content/met/advice/lfr/deployment-records/lfr-deployment-grid-2023-to-2024.pdf ) and 2020 to 2022 ( https://www.met.police.uk/SysSiteAssets/media/downloads/force-content/met/advice/lfr/new/lfr-deployment-grid-2020-2022.pdf ). Each row: deployment location, date, duration, use case, watchlist size, minimum threshold, total alerts, true and false alerts confirmed and unconfirmed, false alert rate, arrests, other outcomes, no-action counts, estimated faces seen. Retrospective only. Note both the Met and BTP web pages sit behind a Cloudflare bot check that returns 403 to automated fetchers; the PDF assets download directly and the pages read fine in a browser. (2) BRITISH TRANSPORT POLICE - https://www.btp.police.uk/police-forces/british-transport-police/areas/about-us/about-us/facial-recognition-technology/ carries BOTH an 'Upcoming deployments' section naming the next station and date and a 'Deployment history and performance' link to the register at https://www.btp.police.uk/SysSiteAssets/media/images/british-transport-police/live-facial-recognition/lfr-deployment-register.pdf . This is the only official London web page found that publishes a forthcoming LFR location. (3) BOROUGH POLICING ACCOUNTS ON X - the Met's actual forward channel, one account per Basic Command Unit, e.g. https://x.com/MPSWestminster , https://x.com/MPSHaringey (see https://x.com/MPSHaringey/status/1986033250536489215 ), https://x.com/MPSCroydon (see https://x.com/MPSCroydon/status/1879477695572021424 ). (4) MET NEWS - https://news.met.police.uk carries results, milestones and strategy announcements, not deployment schedules; e.g. the West End static rollout announcement of 24 June 2026 and the '100 arrests following new Live Facial Recognition pilot in Croydon' item. (5) MET LFR ANNUAL REPORT - https://www.met.police.uk/SysSiteAssets/media/downloads/force-content/met/advice/lfr/other-lfr-documents/live-facial-recognition-annual-report-2025.pdf , published 31 October 2025, aggregate figures and the description of the notification practice. (6) LONDON ASSEMBLY / MAYOR'S QUESTIONS - https://www.london.gov.uk/who-we-are/what-london-assembly-does/questions-mayor/find-an-answer/live-facial-recognition-deployment-locations and the Garbett report at https://www.london.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-02/The%20unchecked%20expansion%20of%20live%20facial%20recognition%20technology%20in%20London%20-%20Zo%C3%AB%20Garbett%20Feb%202026.pdf . (7) MET FOI DISCLOSURE LOG - e.g. https://www.met.police.uk/foi-ai/metropolitan-police/disclosure-2024/april-2024/locations-facial-recognition-cameras-arrests-london-boroughs-2021-2023/ . (8) LOCAL AND NATIONAL PRESS - reliable for large or controversial deployments (Notting Hill Carnival, the May 2026 protest deployments) and useless for routine ones. (9) CAMPAIGN GROUPS - https://bigbrotherwatch.org.uk/campaigns/stop-facial-recognition/ , https://www.libertyhumanrights.org.uk/fundamental/facial-recognition/ ; commentary and FOI-derived analysis, no location feed. City of London Police has no LFR transparency page because it operates no LFR.
live_feed_or_map_available: NO. There is no live map of LFR van positions in London. Not official, not third-party, not campaign-run, not crowdsourced, not commercial - none exists, and nothing was found that is being built. That is the direct answer, and the rest of this field is what is there instead and how stale it is. WHAT THE OFFICIAL SITES ACTUALLY HAVE. The Metropolitan Police's facial recognition page, captured on 3 August 2026, contains exactly four things: policy documents, impact assessments, deployment records and other LFR documents. There is no 'upcoming deployments' heading, no calendar, no map, no feed. The older advice-section page that some sources still cite now 404s. So on the Met's own website the forward-looking answer is nothing at all, despite the MPS Overt LFR Policy section 10 committing that 'the public should be notified of LFR Deployments in advance using the MPS website and other appropriate communication channels (for example social media)', subject to exceptions for urgency and for intelligence-sensitive operations. The commitment is real; the website half of it is not being met in any structured way. British Transport Police is the exception and the one genuinely forward-looking official artefact in London: its LFR page carries an 'Upcoming deployments' block that on 11 August 2026 read, in full, 'Tuesday 11 August - London Victoria Underground station'. One line of prose, one station, same day. THE CLOSEST THING TO A LIVE CHANNEL. For the Met it is the borough Basic Command Unit accounts on X - @MPSWestminster, @MPSHaringey, @MPSCroydon and their equivalents - which post a standard notice naming the borough, sometimes a day or two ahead ('On 5th November, we are deploying Live Facial Recognition Technology to crime hotspots in #Haringey borough'), sometimes on the day. This is the nearest thing to a live signal that exists. It is also close to useless as data: it is scattered across roughly a dozen accounts with no common hashtag or index, it names a borough rather than a street, it gives no time window, it is not archived anywhere searchable, it is not machine-readable, and reading it requires an X account. Physical signage at the zone of recognition is the only other real-time indicator, and by the time you can read it you are already in the zone. WHY NO MAP CAN EASILY BE MADE FROM THE OFFICIAL DATA. Asked directly by Zoe Garbett AM on 18 July 2024 to publish approximate coordinates for each deployment and to include more precise locations in future, the Mayor answered on 30 July 2024 that 'location data for Live Facial Recognition (LFR) deployments is not recorded in coordinate format', adding that the MPS would explore adding greater specificity to the deployment log. Two years on, the 2025 and 2026 records still give free-text labels such as 'Powis St, Woolwich', 'Stratford B'way' and 'High St North, East Ham'. Any map of Met LFR is therefore a geocoding exercise over prose, and its precision is a high street, not a parking spot. WHAT WAS CHECKED AND FOUND EMPTY. Big Brother Watch runs no tracker and no map; its Stop Facial Recognition page says it attends deployments 'when we are tipped off', which is informal intelligence, never published as a feed, and its own deployment table stops in 2023. Liberty and Privacy International publish policy material and no locations. There is no LFR dataset on the London Datastore. No GitHub project scraping the Met's deployment PDFs into a mappable dataset was found. The OpenStreetMap-derived camera maps - Surveillance under Surveillance at https://sunders.uber.space/ and its mirrors - are genuinely live in that they refresh from OSM, and they are the only reusable geographic camera layer that exists, but they show ordinary CCTV; London has effectively no facial-recognition-tagged nodes, so they answer a different question. Surfshark's facial recognition map at https://surfshark.com/facial-recognition-map is country-level policy colouring, not deployments. No app, no bot, no mailing list and no Mastodon or Bluesky feed for London LFR deployments was found. THE CLOSEST SUBSTITUTE AND ITS LAG. For history, the Met deployment records, which are excellent and which lag by weeks to months - the 2025 record's final row is 23 December 2025 and the complete file was in circulation by April 2026, while a legacy copy at the old lfr-deployment-grid.pdf URL was still serving data ending 11 July 2025 as late as 31 July 2026. For the immediate future, BTP's one-line 'Upcoming deployments' notice, which is station-accurate, transport-only, and hours ahead. For the Met's immediate future, a borough X post on the day. Ranked by lag: physical signage, zero minutes, requires being there; borough X post, zero to about 48 hours; BTP upcoming notice, hours; press coverage, same day but only for notable deployments; BTP register, days to weeks; Met deployment record, weeks to months. There is nothing in the zero-lag, remote, machine-readable quadrant, which is exactly the thing a live map would need. Two contrasts worth noting because they show it is not technically impossible: Essex Police has published a forward schedule of deployments through a period weeks ahead, and Surrey Police pledges at least seven days' notice - both outside London, both from smaller forces, both better than anything the Met offers.
advance_notice_period: No force operating in London publishes a guaranteed minimum. Metropolitan Police: policy requires advance notification via the website and other channels but names no period; in practice the Annual Report 2025 describes signage 'on the day' and announcement 'via social media', and observed borough posts range from roughly a day or two ahead to same-day. Effective answer: zero to about 48 hours, unreliable, and nothing at all on the Met's own website. British Transport Police: commits to publishing details on its website before each deployment; observed practice is same-day - the 'Upcoming deployments' entry naming an 11 August 2026 deployment was live on 11 August 2026, and the BTP and TfL announcements went out that day. City of London Police: not applicable. For contrast outside London, Surrey Police pledges at least seven days and Essex Police has published a multi-week forward schedule, so a week of notice is achievable and simply is not being given in London. [uncertain - no force publishes a stated notice period, so every figure here is inferred from dated observations rather than quoted from a commitment]
foi_or_audit_sources: The audit trail that exists is almost entirely built on the Met's own published records rather than on FOI, which is unusual and worth saying plainly - the raw material is already public, it is just not in a usable shape. The most substantial audit is 'The unchecked expansion of live facial recognition technology in London', Zoe Garbett AM, London Assembly, 10 February 2026, which analyses every deployment since 2020 from the Met's records, produces the borough table and a static choropleth map (Figure 2) of deployments by borough, and finds the ward-level racial disproportionality. Its predecessor finding, that over half of 2024 deployments were in areas with a higher-than-average Black population - Thornton Heath in Croydon 40%, Northumberland Park in Haringey 36%, Deptford High Street in Lewisham 34% - is at https://www.london.gov.uk/over-half-all-facial-recognition-deployments-last-year-took-place-areas-higher-proportion-black . Mayor's Question of 18 July 2024, answered 30 July 2024, is the primary source for the Met not recording coordinates. Met FOI disclosures that enumerate locations include 'Locations of facial recognition cameras and arrests in all London boroughs from 2021 to 2023' ( https://www.met.police.uk/foi-ai/metropolitan-police/disclosure-2024/april-2024/locations-facial-recognition-cameras-arrests-london-boroughs-2021-2023/ ), 'Facial recognition deployments in 2022 and 2023' ( https://www.met.police.uk/foi-ai/metropolitan-police/disclosure-2024/july-2024/facial-recognition-deployments-2022-2023/ ) and 'Deployment of Facial Recognition at London events in August and September 2024/2025' ( https://www.met.police.uk/foi-ai/metropolitan-police/disclosure-2025/november-2025/deployment-facial-recognition-london-events-august-september2024-2025/ ). Big Brother Watch's FOI work is the source for the Network Rail AI camera trials and for its February 2026 response to the Home Office consultation on police use of facial recognition; Liberty Investigates reported in December 2025 that children as young as 12 were on police LFR watchlists, with an average of 105 under-18s per watchlist. Statewatch's June 2026 piece 'England: Police use of facial recognition technology growing rapidly' aggregates the national picture.
legal_basis: The duty to publish is soft and self-imposed, which is the root of the problem. It rests on the surveillance camera code of practice made under the Protection of Freedoms Act 2012 - the Met publishes a self-assessment against it - on the transparency principle in Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018 for law enforcement processing, on the requirement flowing from R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058 that the discretion over where LFR is deployed be constrained by published policy, and on each force's own policy. The Met's Overt LFR Policy section 10 is the operative text: policy and impact assessments to be published on the website; the public 'should be notified of LFR Deployments in advance using the MPS website and other appropriate communication channels (for example social media)', with exceptions in cases of urgency and where intelligence sources or operational objectives would be compromised; overtness during deployment via officers who can answer questions, liveried vehicles with signage and signage or an equivalent measure outside the zone of recognition; and, post-deployment, publication of a record confirming for each deployment the location, date, duration, use case, watchlist size, minimum threshold, total alerts, confirmed and unconfirmed true and false alerts, false alert rate and estimated faces passing the system - eleven specified fields, all of which the published records do in fact contain. What is missing is any obligation to publish coordinates, any minimum notice period, any machine-readable format, and any obligation to publish before rather than after.
regulatory_challenges: The transparency question has now been litigated and the police won. In Thompson and Carlo v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis, judgment 21 April 2026, the High Court (Lord Justice Holgate and Mrs Justice Farbey) upheld the lawfulness of the Met's 2024 LFR policy, finding it contained 'clear, interlocking and cumulative constraints' and rejecting the argument that it left officers too much discretion over where, why and against whom LFR is used, contrary to Articles 8, 10 and 11 ECHR. Shaun Thompson - a community worker misidentified as his brother, stopped and threatened with arrest - and Silkie Carlo of Big Brother Watch both said they would appeal; the judgment summary is at https://www.judiciary.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Summary-of-judgment-Thomson-and-Carlo-v-Metropolitan-Police-Commmissioner-AC-2024-LON-001764-21-04-2026.pdf . The practical consequence for this item is that the current publication regime - retrospective records, same-day social media, no coordinates, no forward website listing - has been held to be legally sufficient, so it is unlikely to improve without political or legislative pressure. That pressure exists: the Equality and Human Rights Commission has said the Met's use must comply with human rights law; Zoe Garbett AM has called for an immediate pause and for full publication of costs; and the Home Office consultation on a legal framework for police facial recognition, to which Big Brother Watch responded in February 2026, is where a statutory publication duty could be created. Bridges remains the governing authority on constraining deployment discretion.
oversight_body: No single body oversees the publication of LFR locations, which is why the standard varies by force. The Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime and the London Assembly Police and Crime Committee scrutinise the Met, and the Mayor has stated that 'it is important that this technology is deployed proportionately, lawfully and ethically and that the MPS is transparent about where, when and how it is used' - but the Mayor also stresses that deployment decisions are operational and that neither he nor MOPAC makes them. The Information Commissioner's Office covers the data protection dimension. The functions of the former Biometrics and Surveillance Camera Commissioner, under whose code of practice the Met publishes its self-assessment, were absorbed elsewhere under the Data Protection and Digital Information reforms, leaving no dedicated surveillance camera regulator. The London Policing Ethics Panel reported on Met LFR and the Met published a response. British Transport Police answers to the British Transport Police Authority. The National Physical Laboratory tests the algorithm but has no remit over transparency. In short, oversight of what gets published is fragmented across MOPAC, the Assembly, the ICO and each force's own governance, with nobody empowered to require a common format, a coordinate, or a day's notice.
key_uncertainties: The central negative finding - that no live map of LFR van positions exists anywhere - is as firmly established as a negative can be. It was checked against the Met's own site (including an archived capture of the current facial recognition page), BTP's site and register, City of London Police, the GLA and Mayor's Question archive, the London Datastore, Big Brother Watch, Liberty, Privacy International, OpenStreetMap-derived camera maps, GitHub, and general and targeted web search, and nothing turned up. Six specific gaps remain. (1) The 2026 Met deployment record could not be read: both met.police.uk and btp.police.uk sit behind a Cloudflare interstitial that returns 403 to automated fetchers, and the 2026 PDF is not in the Wayback Machine either, so the exact number of 2026 deployments and how current that file is were inferred rather than counted - it should be opened manually in a browser. (2) The Met's advance-notice period is inferred from three dated borough X posts and the Annual Report's 'on the day' wording; no force publishes a stated minimum, so 'zero to about 48 hours' is an observation, not a quotation. (3) It could not be confirmed whether every Met deployment gets a borough post or only some - if coverage is partial, the practical forward-notice rate is worse than it looks. (4) X posts could not be retrieved directly (the API returns 402), so the three cited permalinks come from search result metadata and their full text was not read end to end. (5) A closed or invite-only community tracker - a Signal group, a Discord, a private mailing list - would not be visible to this method, and Big Brother Watch's 'when we are tipped off' language implies exactly such informal networks exist; the finding is that nothing PUBLIC exists, which is a slightly narrower claim. (6) Whether the Met's promise to 'explore how to incorporate greater specificity to deployment locations' has produced anything since July 2024 could not be tested without reading the 2026 record. For the cammap project specifically: the cameras list here is deliberately empty because this item is about channels, not sites - the mappable site-level data lives in the Met and BTP items of this survey - and because the Met does not record deployment locations as coordinates at all, so any van layer built from these records is a geocode of free-text street names, accurate to a high street and never to a parking position, and should be labelled as such rather than drawn as a precise dot.

sources.what_it_supports: PRIMARY AND DECISIVE for the publication duty. Section 10 'Transparency and reporting': policy and impact assessments published on the website; Pre-Deployment - 'The public should be notified of LFR Deployments in advance using the MPS website and other appropriate communication channels (for example social media)', with exceptions for urgency and intelligence sensitivity; During a Deployment - officers able to answer questions, MPS-liveried vehicles with signage, signage or equivalent outside the zone of recognition; Post-Deployment - the eleven fields the Met undertakes to publish for every deployment, which match the deployment record columns exactly. sources.title: The unchecked expansion of live facial recognition technology in London - Zoe Garbett AM (PDF)
sources.what_it_supports: The best independent audit of the deployment records and the nearest thing to a map that exists: Figure 2, a static choropleth of deployments by borough since 2020. Source of the borough table (Westminster 75, Croydon 55, Newham 35, down to Barnet 1), the per-100,000 rates, the 263-to-180 ward disproportionality finding, the OIFR budget contradiction, and the transparency critique.

sources.title: MPS Haringey deployment notice on X
sources.date: posted ahead of a 5 November deployment
sources.what_it_supports: The Met's actual forward channel, in its standard wording and in the future tense: 'On 5th November, we are deploying Live Facial Recognition Technology to crime hotspots in #Haringey borough', with links to the Met's LFR information and to the watchlist policy. Borough-level, no street, no time window. Companion examples: https://x.com/MPSCroydon/status/1879477695572021424 (Croydon, 15 January 2025) and @MPSWestminster (Westminster, 3 September 2026).

sources.title: Stop Facial Recognition - Big Brother Watch
sources.what_it_supports: PRIMARY for the negative finding on the campaign side. Big Brother Watch publishes no map, no tracker, no deployment schedule and no dataset; it documents deployments after the fact, and states that 'when we are tipped off about future facial recognition deployments we attend to demonstrate'. Contact is by newsletter, email or Signal. Its own deployment statistics table at https://bigbrotherwatch.org.uk/blog/understanding-live-facial-recognition-statistics/ stops in 2023.

sources.title: Summary of judgment, Thompson and Carlo v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis (PDF)
sources.what_it_supports: The High Court upholding the Met's 2024 LFR policy as containing 'clear, interlocking and cumulative constraints', rejecting the Article 8/10/11 challenge over discretion as to where and against whom LFR is used. Establishes that the current publication regime has been held legally sufficient. Shaun Thompson and Silkie Carlo both stated an intention to appeal.

sources.title: Met makes one arrest every 35 minutes during live facial recognition pilot
sources.what_it_supports: What news.met.police.uk actually carries - results and milestones, not deployment schedules. The Croydon static pilot October 2025 to March 2026, 24 operations, 173 arrests, more than 470,000 people passing the cameras with one false alert. Companion: the 24 June 2026 West End and Soho static rollout announcement at https://news.met.police.uk/news/met-commissioner-to-announce-plans-to-introduce-lfr-into-crime-hotspots-across-the-west-end-510675 .

sources.title: Surveillance under Surveillance (OpenStreetMap-derived camera map)
sources.what_it_supports: The only live, reusable, crowdsourced camera map that exists for London - and the evidence that it does not answer this question. It renders OSM surveillance nodes (fixed CCTV, dome cameras, ANPR) contributed by volunteers, refreshed from OSM, with an open contribution route. It carries no facial recognition layer and no LFR van data, and its own documentation warns that coverage is partial and needs verification.

sources.title: Locations of facial recognition cameras and arrests in all London boroughs from 2021 to 2023 (Met FOI disclosure)
sources.what_it_supports: That the FOI route produces the same free-text location granularity as the published records rather than anything more precise, and that the Met's standard FOI answer is to point back at the published deployment records.
